Belief
bē-lēf´
n. (the assent and trust of the heart; the instrument by which salvation is received)
From Old English geleafa, related to lief, dear — belief is what a man holds dear enough to rest on. The KJV uses the noun once, at 2 Thessalonians 2:13, rendering Greek pistis, elsewhere and usually translated faith.

Biblical Definition

Paul sets belief inside a chain that begins before the world: “But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth” (2 Thessalonians 2:13). Election is the source, the Spirit's sanctifying work is the means, and belief of the truth is the instrument — and the truth is an object, not a mood; a man believes something. Belief is therefore never a work a sinner performs to earn the choosing; it is the appointed way the chosen receive what was given. Its beginnings can be very small and very honest: “And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief” (Mark 9:24) — and Christ healed the boy. Yet the thing itself is indispensable: “But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him” (Hebrews 11:6). And its origin is outside the believer: “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). Belief is not the cause of the new birth but its first breath.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines belief as a persuasion of the truth, or an assent of mind to the truth of a declaration — and in theology, faith, or a firm persuasion of the truths of religion.

expand to see more

BELIEF, n. A persuasion of the truth, or an assent of mind to the truth of a declaration, proposition or alleged fact, on the ground of evidence.

BELIEF, n. In theology, faith, or a firm persuasion of the truths of religion.

BELIEF, n. The thing believed; the object of belief; as, the creed contains the belief of the church.

BELIEVE, v.t. To credit upon the authority or testimony of another; to expect or hope with confidence; to trust.

UNBELIEF, n. Incredulity; the withholding of belief. In theology, disbelief of the truth of the gospel.

Key Scripture

2 Thessalonians 2:13 — "But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth:"

Mark 9:24 — "And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."

Hebrews 11:6 — "But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him."

Romans 10:17 — "So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God."

Modern Corruption

Belief is emptied of content and reduced to a posture — believing in oneself, or believing in believing — so that a word with an object becomes a word with none.

expand to see more

Modern usage has made belief intransitive. A man is told to believe, and nothing follows the verb; the recommended object is his own capacity or the goodness of the universe. Paul writes belief of the truth, with a genitive that will not come off. Hebrews 11:6 specifies two propositions the comer must hold — that God is, and that He rewards those who seek Him. A belief with no content is not weak faith; it is a different thing wearing the word.

Romans 10:17 closes the other exit. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God, which makes belief a response to something said from outside the man. It cannot be worked up in a meeting by intensity, nor manufactured by deciding hard enough. This is also the comfort of the doctrine. Mark 9:24 is the honest confession of a man whose faith was mixed with its opposite, said with tears, and the Lord did not send him away to acquire a better grade of it first.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek pistis (G4102), faith, belief; pisteuo (G4100), to believe, trust; apistia (G570), unbelief; aletheia (G225), truth.

expand to see more

Greek pistis (G4102) — faith; rendered belief at 2 Thessalonians 2:13, faith elsewhere.

Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, to entrust oneself to; the verb of John 3:16.

Greek apistia (G570) — unbelief; Mark 9:24, what the father confessed alongside his faith.

Greek aletheia (G225) — truth; the object belief must have to be belief.

Greek hagiasmos (G38) — sanctification; the Spirit's work named with belief in the same clause.

Usage

"“Belief of the truth” — a genitive that will not come off."

"“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief” — honest, mixed, and accepted."

"“Faith cometh by hearing” — from outside the man, never worked up within him."
